justification: Capped at 7.0 by one verifiable misquotation; without the cap this is about 9.2, and would be the strongest article of its kind I have reviewed against the field. Against the comparison set, this page is in a different league: freeCodeCamp's SOLID walkthrough uses Java, abstract-ish domains (bookstore invoice, parking lot, Rectangle/Square for LSP), and shows before/after code with no execution or real output; Wikipedia's SOLID page is pure prose definition with zero code. This article instead gives five distinct, original, running C# domains (library fine notice, shipping-rate pricer, BCL ReadOnlyCollection/IList<T>, report exporter, receipt printer), each with a genuine violation, a demonstrated consequence, and a fix, all machine-verified by tools/run-code.mjs (26 blocks, 14 executed, PASS on 3 consecutive runs). I independently re-derived all five violation-to-consequence narratives with my own standalone .NET 10 programs rather than trusting the article's output blocks: (1) SRP - confirmed daysLate*0.25m is byte-for-byte identical in both BuildNotice versions and that CheckFine fails only because it substring-matches the reworded sentence, not because the fine changed; (2) OCP - confirmed 'StandardPlus'.StartsWith('Standard') is true and that the naive chain silently returns the Standard rate (1.0m) instead of 1.5m for the new tier; (3) LSP - built my own List<int>.AsReadOnly() referenced through IList<int> and called .Add(40): it throws System.NotSupportedException with message 'Collection is read-only.', exactly matching the article's claim, and confirmed IReadOnlyList<int> makes the same call a compile error, CS1061, with the exact message text the article quotes; (4) ISP - ran the fat-interface batch loop myself and confirmed the third array element (the second SalesReport, listed right after QuickSummaryReport) never executes because the unhandled NotImplementedException from QuickSummaryReport kills the foreach entirely, not just that one iteration; (5) DIP - ran the static-Muted version myself and confirmed both Process calls produce zero output: the interactive Order-202 call is silently muted by state the earlier batch call left behind, with no exception to notice. All five are genuinely real, not staged, and the ISP and DIP cases in particular (a whole loop dying past a report, one order's global flag silently killing an unrelated later order) are sharper failure modes than anything in the comparison set. Source-checking: I fetched every distinct source used for a direct quotation. Martin's 'Solid Relevance' quotes for SRP, OCP, LSP, and ISP all check out verbatim. Microsoft Learn's ReadOnlyCollection<T> page confirms the five interfaces listed and the exact 'This implementation always throws NotSupportedException' language for Add/Clear/Remove/Insert/RemoveAt. Microsoft Learn's architectural-principles page confirms the DIP paragraph verbatim, including the correctly-ellipsised quote. Seemann's 'Interfaces Aren't Abstractions' confirms 'An interface is just a language construct. In essence, it's just a shape', the Header Interfaces definition, the Extract Interface remark, and the single-implementation code smell claim. Fowler's Yagni page confirms both quotes verbatim. The DIP-vs-DI-container section is accurate and the Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection demo wires the identical IReceiptPrinter/ConsoleReceiptPrinter/OrderProcessor triple used in the hand-written DIP fix, not a different example - a real, common point of confusion drawn correctly. The over-applied section is a genuine, reasoned critique (not a token paragraph): it correctly distinguishes the article's own retroactively-justified IShippingRate extraction (two real implementations already exist) from a hypothetical pre-emptive one, and is internally consistent with the fixes earlier in the piece. Against this generally strong picture, one quotation does not hold up: the LSP section says IList<T>'s IsReadOnly is 'documented as meaning that "these mutation methods should throw" when it is true [[5]]', in quotation marks, cited to the IList<T> interface page. I checked that page's full Remarks (very short, no mention of IsReadOnly semantics), the inherited ICollection<T>.IsReadOnly property page's Remarks ('A collection that is read-only does not allow the addition or removal of elements after the collection is created' - different wording, no 'should throw'), the ICollection<T> interface page's own Remarks, and IList<T>.Insert's Exceptions section ('The IList<T> is read-only.' triggers NotSupportedException, again different wording). The phrase 'these mutation methods should throw' does not appear verbatim anywhere I could find in the cited source or its closest neighbours; the underlying claim is true in substance (the Exceptions sections do document NotSupportedException), but presenting a paraphrase inside quotation marks as if it were Microsoft's own wording is the same category of error the four-pillars-of-oop round-1 review flagged as major (an invented word inside a quoted C# spec sentence). Two smaller findings: the front-matter source [1] ('The Single Responsibility Principle', 2014) is never cited inline anywhere in the article - only [2] 'Solid Relevance' is used, including for the SRP section's own opening Martin quote - which the editorial brief calls a finding in its own right. And the sentence attributing the OCP phrasing to 'Bertrand Meyer's original phrasing, quoted in Martin's own summary' cites [[2]], but Martin's Solid-Relevance post never names Meyer anywhere on the page; the attribution is true and well known (Meyer, Object-Oriented Software Construction, 1988) but the citation given doesn't itself support it.

issues.location: 'Liskov substitution: a violation the BCL ships with', paragraph beginning "`IList<T>` itself anticipates this", the quoted fragment '"these mutation methods should throw"' cited to [[5]]
issues.problem: Misquotation. The sentence puts "these mutation methods should throw" in quotation marks and cites the IList<T> interface page [[5]] as the source. I fetched that page's full Remarks section (a single sentence describing inheritance from ICollection<T>, nothing about IsReadOnly semantics), the ICollection<T>.IsReadOnly property page's Remarks ('A collection that is read-only does not allow the addition or removal of elements after the collection is created'), the ICollection<T> interface page's Remarks, and IList<T>.Insert's Exceptions section ('The IList<T> is read-only.' -> NotSupportedException). None of them contain the phrase "these mutation methods should throw", or anything close to it verbatim. The underlying claim (IsReadOnly=true implies mutation throws NotSupportedException) is correct and well documented elsewhere on the page (the Exceptions sections), but the specific quoted wording does not exist in the cited source.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote something that actually appears verbatim (e.g. IList<T>.Insert's Exceptions entry: "The IList<T> is read-only."), or drop the quotation marks and state the claim in the article's own words: "documented, across Add/Insert/Remove/RemoveAt's Exceptions sections, to throw NotSupportedException when IsReadOnly is true [[5]]".
